*"Don't you miss having a strong man's shoulder to lean on?"* Rebecca223 asked, with a hundred-dollar donation. *"Would you give up your business if you met the love of your life?"*

Freya decided to answer.

"A business can't replace a man, and a man can't replace your life's work. Though you don't have to please a business the way you do a lover. And the right business can *always* keep it up for you"—here Freya smiled—"which, you have to admit, gives it a distinct advantage over a man."

The chats exploded. The Twitter and Instagram feeds on her side monitors raced like mad. The feminist community mobilized in full force, and the feed suddenly bloomed with avatars with multicolored hair, like an exotic conservatory. Now it wasn't her assistants but Freya's own fans filing reports and tearing into the right-wingers who had swarmed toward the light of her stream from their anonymous loser forums. Right-wingers were always a massive headache.

Still, three hundred and eighty... no, three hundred and ninety thousand live viewers were still three hundred and ninety thousand viewers. No matter what they smelled like.

The trolls tried to flood the broadcast with questions like *"Do you suck dick?"* and *"Try shaving your legs"*: zero imagination, pure volume. Stupid sad green frogs began popping up in the chat. Freya kept smiling and selectively answering questions while glancing over at her assistants' chat. Like it or not, the comments set the tone. As it turned out, though, the moderators' help wasn't needed.

The trolls' moms didn't give them more than five dollars for school lunch. So they were utterly crushed by a counterattack from the very core of Freya's audience, rallying to the call of fan groups across Twitter, TikTok, and Instagram. Rushing to their idol's rescue came moms on maternity leave, nail techs, and small-town college girls. Housewives who, answering the clarion call of the modern economy, had traded their ladles for giant smartphones. And also the men who craved the attention of all the aforementioned women, and so had started pretending to be "one of them," without even noticing how they were blowing twenty bucks a month, or even more, on Freya.

Not the finest audience if you're a serious woman sharing the secrets of *real* success, sure—but a loyal one. And loyalty counts for plenty in real business.

Right before Freya's eyes, the haters' comments were washed away by twenty- and fifty-dollar messages: *"Go, Freya!", "Freya, we love you!", "#Axelsensexuals!"* The stakes rose rapidly, and before long, donations under ten dollars didn't even appear on screen. At last, the young woman gave a genuine smile.
